title: 'Misinformation? What of it?' Motivations and Individual Differences in Misinformation Sharing on Social Media
screen_reason: The paper's aim is motivations and personality correlates, but its 'Misinformation: Awareness and Behavior' section reports two descriptive shares of respondents with the full sample as denominator: 67.8% (116/171) say they had themselves shared misinformation on social media, and 94.7% (162/171) say they had seen other people share misinformation. Both are self-reported shares of survey respondents, i.e. RECALL (sharing and exposure). A study whose aim is something else is still included when a descriptive share is reported.

estimates.country: Not stated in the methods; the questionnaire was distributed 'around the campuses of two universities using convenience sampling'. Both authors are at the Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information, Nanyang Technological University, 31 Nanyang Link, Singapore 637718
estimates.platform: social media in general (the introduction names Twitter and Facebook as examples); respondents reported across platforms, 74.8% used more than one
estimates.date: Not reported; paper presented at ASIST 2013, 1-6 November 2013
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have themselves shared misinformation on social media
estimates.value_raw: n = 116, 67.8% of 171 ('more than two-thirds of the respondents')
estimates.denominator: 171 university students under 30 years old who were social media users, recruited by convenience sampling on the campuses of two universities (all 171 used social media; 81.3% daily)
estimates.definition: Respondent indicated that they had shared misinformation on social media themselves. No time window was specified. Respondents were given the definition of misinformation plus 'concrete examples ... to give respondents a clear sense of what misinformation means'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation - defined as information that has been shown to be inaccurate - is rampant in this medium (Karlova & Fisher, 2013)"; the questionnaire also supplied concrete examples.
estimates.source_quote: more than two-thirds of the respondents (n = 116, 67.8%)
estimates.page_loc: Findings, subsection 'Misinformation: Awareness and Behavior'; also stated in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondents' own judgement, on a pilot-tested self-administered questionnaire (paper and electronic) that supplied a definition of misinformation ('information that has been shown to be inaccurate') and concrete examples. No external verification of what respondents counted as misinformation and no reliability statistic for this behavioural item (the reported Cronbach's alphas 0.77-0.90 belong to the four motivation factors, not to this item).
estimates.moderator_quote: The respondents were university students under 30 years old who were social media users. This population was selected because they tend to be comfortable with social media and technology. Participation was voluntary. Hard copies of the questionnaire were distributed around the campuses of two universities using convenience sampling. An electronic version was also available to the participants.
estimates.notes: 116/171 = 67.8% checks out exactly. TWO CODING CALLS FOR THE ADJUDICATOR. (a) country_norm 'Singapore' is INFERRED from the author affiliation (Nanyang Technological University, Singapore) and the fact that the questionnaire was handed out on two university campuses; the paper never names the country of data collection. If the review forbids inferring country from affiliation, this becomes unspecified. (b) topic coded 'other' because the questionnaire placed no topical restriction on 'misinformation' - it is any inaccurate information shared on social media, not specifically news; an adjudicator preferring a catch-all for unrestricted topics would code general_news. Data-collection dates are never given; year is the conference/publication year 2013, so the underlying behaviour is from 2012-2013. QUOTE NOTE: the text file is a two-column rendering in which every body line carries text from BOTH columns, so a multi-line sentence cannot be quoted contiguously; the source_quote is therefore the single line carrying the value. The full sentence as printed reads: 'Nevertheless, more than two-thirds of the respondents (n = 116, 67.8%) indicated that they had shared misinformation on social media themselves.'

estimates.notes: 162/171 = 94.7% checks out exactly. This is an encounter/witnessing item ('seen other people share misinformation'), so recall_subtype = exposure, not sharing; it is not a definition variant of the 67.8% row but a different measure (seeing others vs. doing it oneself). Same country and topic caveats as the other row. Note the ceiling-level value: with no time window and no frequency threshold ('had seen', ever), 94.7% is a lifetime any-exposure figure and is not comparable to windowed exposure items. missed_or_uncertain: Seen and NOT extracted. (1) Perceived importance of truthfulness when sharing (M = 3.85 on a 1-5 scale, SD = 0.97) - a scale mean with no share of respondents, so no row per the instructions. (2) All 16 motivation item means (top three: get others' opinions 5.02, express own opinion 4.95, interact with others 4.89; lowest: be first to share 3.37, look good 3.48, feel influential 3.74) and the four factor scores - these are motivations for sharing, measured on 7-point agreement scales, not shares of respondents and not prevalence. (3) Sample-description shares that are not about misinformation: 81.3% using social media every day, 74.8% using more than one platform, the gender and undergraduate/graduate splits. (4) Regression betas (extraversion .25 on the socializing factor, conscientiousness -.16 on self-expression/status seeking) and the R2 values 0.20-0.29. (5) DATA-QUALITY FLAG for the adjudicator: the sample description is internally inconsistent - 'more female (n = 86, 60.2%) than male respondents (n = 68, 39.8%)' gives 86 + 68 = 154, not 171, and 86/171 = 50.3%, not 60.2%. The two values extracted here are unaffected (116/171 = 67.8% and 162/171 = 94.7% both reproduce exactly), but the discrepancy is worth recording as a reporting-accuracy signal for this paper.

rob.design: Cross-sectional self-administered questionnaire, 171 university students under 30 who were social media users, recruited by convenience sampling on the campuses of two universities; hard copies plus an electronic version; participation voluntary; questionnaire pilot tested and containing 16 motivation items, the 44-item Big Five Inventory, demographics, and behaviour items on misinformation sharing, with concrete examples of misinformation supplied. Analysis: descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis with varimax rotation (KMO = .88; Bartlett chi-square(120, N = 171) = 1742.06, p = .000; four factors, 72.55% of variance; Cronbach's alpha .77-.90) and four multiple regressions, in SPSS. Weaknesses: no country of data collection stated, no data-collection dates, no response rate, convenience student sample, no external verification of self-reported misinformation, no reliability statistic for the two behavioural items used here, and an internal inconsistency in the reported gender counts (86 + 68 = 154, not 171).
